messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 33
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Prosecutor
  trauma_type: Terrorism
  pcl5: 56

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Feeling Tired: Feeling very tired or exhausted, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell, Auditory (Explosion): Explosion or bang sounds
  Memory: No Coherent Story: I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself, More Real Than Normal: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things, Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
  Negative Appraisals: Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened, Distrust Others: People are not what they seem, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Liam, a 33-year-old prosecutor, presented for an initial consultation at the urging of his wife, reporting that he "wasn't himself" since the festival bombing six months prior. He spoke in a measured, almost detached tone, as if presenting facts in a courtroom, yet his tightly clenched hands betrayed a deep and persistent distress. The event itself remains a constellation of sensory fragments rather than a coherent narrative. He can recall the bone-deep exhaustion he felt that evening, a weariness from a long day in the sun that had settled in his limbs. He remembers the cloying, sweet smell of beer someone had spilled on the grass nearby. Then there is the memory of the sound—not just a bang, but a physical force that seemed to tear the air apart. These pieces exist in his mind with a terrifying clarity, feeling more real and immediate to him now than the memory of his own wedding day. When these flashes occur, it is not like watching a film of the past; he is there again, feeling the ground shudder beneath his feet, the world dissolving into screaming and smoke. He is unable to connect these moments into a story he can tell himself, let alone his wife. The sequence of events is lost, leaving only a chaotic loop of the most horrific seconds.

In the months that followed, Liam’s world began to shrink. He had always been defined by his sharp, analytical mind and his belief in order, but he now found himself governed by a profound sense of threat and self-recrimination. He had come to believe that people are not what they seem, that a placid exterior can hide monstrous intentions. This conviction stemmed from a specific, haunting image from just before the explosion: a man in the crowd, seemingly unremarkable, who had briefly met his gaze. Liam, trained to observe detail, had registered something amiss but dismissed it. This fleeting moment has become the anchor for his guilt. He is certain he should have known, should have acted, should have protected the people around him. The thought, "I should have protected others and I failed," is a constant, punishing refrain. He feels he will never forgive himself for not doing more, for not being the protector his professional identity demanded he be.

This internal state has reshaped his daily existence. As a prosecutor, his office is in the heart of the city, and the sudden backfire of a truck on the street below can send him into a state of immediate panic, the sound indistinguishable from the blast itself. He has started taking different, longer routes to work to avoid crowded plazas. At social functions, the smell of alcohol, once innocuous, now triggers a wave of nausea and a desperate need to escape, a reaction that has strained relationships with colleagues and friends who don't understand his abrupt departures. The exhaustion he once felt only after a long day has become a trigger in itself; when he works late and feels that familiar weariness seep into his bones, the intrusive memories return with renewed force. Consequently, he has started avoiding the very fatigue that his demanding job creates, a paradox that leaves him perpetually on edge. His work, once a source of pride, has become a minefield of suspicion. He looks at witnesses, defendants, and even jurors with a pervasive distrust, seeing potential deceit in every gesture.

Liam sought therapy after his wife found him sitting in his car in their garage, unable to come inside after a particularly difficult day at the courthouse. He confessed to her that he felt he was failing at everything—as a husband, as a lawyer, as a man who was supposed to uphold justice and safety. He is terrified that this new reality, a world of hidden threats and personal failure, is permanent. He hopes therapy can help him find a way to live with the memory, but what he fears most is that he will never again be the man who believed in the fundamental goodness of others, or in his own capacity to protect them.
